name: Amira Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government, and this is confidential. What do you do on a usual day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Amira Mensah, 43, and I'm a junior worker doing carpentry and general tasks on building sites. I left school early, so I've had to learn drawings and cuts while other people are already working fast; I still need the lead to check my setting-out. I bring in boards, build simple frames and tidy the work area. I like seeing a stairwell we finished open to people, but I hate when a rushed measurement sends us back to the saw.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your situation outside the site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ben works evenings in a hotel kitchen, and our children are nine and thirteen. We have a mortgage and about five months of expenses in savings, built from both wages. My pay is about normal for construction here and there are some other builders nearby. I use AI every day to turn photos of marked-up plans into a list of questions, then I ask the lead before cutting; the machine is quick, but I'm still the learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the phone has saved me from forgetting questions, even if AI never does more than that. A phone can catch a wrong number, but it cannot hold the tape measure. I still want the lead beside me when I check the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep my site wage if building carries on. The five-month reserve helps, but Ben's hotel shifts change with bookings, and our mortgage would be hard to carry on one wage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the present shifts and continue turning each plan photo into a question list on my phone. In the first year I'd mark which AI suggestions were wrong in a notebook and show the lead, so I learn the drawing rather than copying a confident error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly about our existing bills. A small AI tool helps me work; it doesn't make Ben's rota or the mortgage predictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the AI get wrong recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It read a handwritten 6 as an 8 on a stair drawing. I asked the lead to check it, and we found the right dimension before anyone cut the timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your coworkers mind the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some laugh, but the lead likes it when I arrive with clear questions instead of guessing. I put the phone away when we're lifting boards together.

I would still ask the lead to check a **wall** with a tape measure.
think: My **site wage** looks likely to continue if building work holds.
Ben’s **hotel shifts** vary, so one wage cannot carry the mortgage for long.
do: Keep **paid site shifts** and use AI to list questions from plans.
Record **wrong AI readings** in a notebook and show the lead.
feel: **Uneasy** about household bills despite a helpful small tool.
S0.quote: A phone can catch a wrong number, but it cannot hold the tape measure.
fieldNote: Amira uses **AI daily** to ask better questions, not to hide that she still needs her lead’s checks.
Her **five-month savings** buffer sits alongside a variable hotel income and a mortgage that needs both wages.

steps.text: Keep working paid carpentry shifts on current sites
Turn marked-up plan photos into AI question lists and log errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the crew to test the new delivery plan before the contractor locks it in. If AI makes office work quicker, workers should share in the saved time instead of being given impossible targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see myself helping check plans because I already use AI on them, but I'm still a junior hand, not the person a builder must keep. If faster planning cuts one helper from each crew, my hours could be the ones to go, and Ben's variable shifts would make the mortgage tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask to test the ordering tool on one small stair job and compare its list with what arrives. In the first year I'd take a paid course in reading plans if offered, keep my normal shifts, and join coworkers asking for published staffing and hour targets before the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like trying a tool first, but I don't like being told it saves labour without being told whose labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure on the stair job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of boards ordered, the number we return, and the hours spent waiting. If the list improves those figures, I'll say so at the site meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for published targets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A target written down can be challenged when an old stairwell is crooked. A target whispered to one worker at a time just makes everyone blame themselves.

say: I would ask for a **site trial** before software delivery plans become fixed.
I would seek **shared savings** rather than impossible labour targets.
think: My **junior hours** could be cut if faster planning shrinks crews.
Ben’s variable **hotel shifts** make a long cut in my pay dangerous.
do: Test an **AI order list** on one stair job.
Join coworkers asking for **written staffing targets**.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours despite interest in the tool.
S1.quote: I don't like being told it saves labour without being told whose labour.
fieldNote: She tests AI with **counts and hours**, looking for evidence before agreeing that productivity has improved.
Her own **junior post** is exposed to smaller crews, and she seeks published targets through coworkers as well as paid instruction.

steps.text: Test AI ordering list on a small stair job this month
Take paid plan-reading course if contractor offers it
Join coworkers requesting written staffing and hour targets
Keep normal paid shifts while the tool is tested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children that the phone I use is not the thing on this card: AGI in 2028 can do nearly all thinking work, and hands-on robots follow around 2031. Our crew has to plan for both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My plan-photo trick would be ordinary once AGI does drawings and orders for less than people. I might still carry and fit on site in 2028, but by 2031 I expect my junior shifts could vanish; five months saved is nowhere near enough for a long mortgage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd ask the union training fund about a paid placement in building safety inspections, and I'd apply only if it includes wages. In 2029 I'd keep site shifts, use AGI to check my written questions and apply for a paid caretaker or repairs position if inspection places are full; if hours fell, Ben and I would call the lender straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can learn fast, but I cannot turn five months of cash into a new wage just by learning a phone menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could inspection be automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, especially the reports and rules. I would test whether there are paid site visits and human checks left; robots after 2031 could narrow that too. I don't want to tell Ben a certificate is a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the children's activities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the paid swimming lessons first and keep the school meals and mortgage covered. I would tell the children why the swimming stopped without asking them to solve an adult bill.

say: I would explain **2028 AGI** and **2031 robots** as different changes to our crew.
I would ask the **union fund** about paid inspection placements.
think: My **plan-reading edge** disappears when AGI handles drawings.
My **junior site wage** could disappear around 2031, outlasting our reserve.
do: Apply for a **paid inspection placement** if wages are included.
Keep **site shifts** and use AGI to check questions in 2029.
Apply for **paid caretaker work** if inspection places are full.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage gap far longer than savings.
S2.quote: I cannot turn five months of cash into a new wage just by learning a phone menu.
fieldNote: Daily AI use makes her alert to **2028 thinking work** changes, but she expects the largest wage blow from physical robots.
She treats inspection as **uncertain**, seeking wages during training and a second application route if places are full.

steps.text: Apply to union fund for paid building-inspection placement if wages included
Keep paid site shifts through 2029 while available
Use AGI to check written site questions in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is enough time to run a proper trial of another paid role, provided contractors open the door. AGI changes plans in 2031; robots that can do the fitting come about 2034, when I will still need to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could lose some helper hours when AGI writes plans, yet site work may keep me employed until physical robots arrive. At 51 in 2034, I expect fitting crews to be smaller; a five-month reserve gives us time to change jobs, not time to wait for a new one to appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid first-aid and site-safety course over the next year if the union fund covers the fees and release time. By 2032 I'd apply for a site safety assistant post and keep my carpentry shifts; in the first year after AGI arrives I'd use it to organise inspection notes, but have a supervisor check every safety call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I feel less rushed. Five years gives me a chance to prove I can spot hazards on real sites before asking anyone to hire me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why safety work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I spotted an unsecured edge before the plasterboard came up, and the lead thanked me. A course alone won't make me an expert, but that moment made me want supervised practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots change safety jobs too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. AGI could write the reports and robots could inspect edges, so I would keep asking what paid tasks remain instead of calling safety a forever job.

say: I would ask for **paid role trials** before robots reach the tools.
I would distinguish **2031 plans** from **2034 fitting**.
think: My **helper hours** may thin after AGI handles plans.
My **site wage** could fall when capable robots shrink fitting crews.
do: Take a funded **site-safety course** if release time is paid.
Apply for a **safety assistant** post by 2032 while working shifts.
Use **AGI inspection notes** with supervisor checks after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to demonstrate skills on real sites.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a chance to prove I can spot hazards on real sites before asking anyone to hire me for it.
fieldNote: Her safety interest comes from a **specific site hazard**, while she admits reports and inspections may later be automated.
She wants **supervised practice** and a funded course without relinquishing the wages needed for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our older child that a decade is plenty of time to learn a trade, but no trade gets a permanent promise. I'll be 53 at AGI in 2036 and 56 when robots reach the tools around 2039; Ben and I still need wages then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be nineteen and twenty-three by 2036, so their school-day costs will change even if they still need help starting out. I can build a better work record over ten years, but physical robots could still reduce site jobs after 2039; I cannot assume a pension or my children's wages will carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid site work now and add a small fixed amount from each pay packet to savings. Over the decade I'd take supervised safety shifts when available and document what I actually checked; in 2037 I'd use AGI to draft inspection notes while applying for full-time safety posts, then compare the pay with my construction wage before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened today. I have years to build proof, but I don't want my children to think a phone skill alone secures their parents' mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you advise your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to choose training with real paid placements and to ask who sets the pay. One might choose a trade, the other college; I wouldn't choose for them just because AI scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run your own inspection business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after I had a qualification, supervised work and paying clients. Right now I am a junior site worker; a logo on a van would not make my safety judgment sound.

say: I would urge my children to seek **paid placements** in any training.
I would explain that **56** still leaves Ben and me needing wages.
think: My children’s **school costs** change as they become adults.
My **site work** may shrink after 2039 despite a longer preparation period.
do: Add a fixed amount to **savings** from each pay packet.
Take **supervised safety shifts** when offered and log checks.
Use **AGI notes** and apply for safety posts in 2037.
feel: **Uneasy** about later wages, with time to build evidence.
S4.quote: Right now I am a junior site worker; a logo on a van would not make my safety judgment sound.
fieldNote: She sees a decade as time for **supervised safety work**, not a licence to call herself an expert or assume a pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most. I could lose my small planning advantage quickly and then lose site shifts to robots around 2031, while the mortgage keeps coming. Paid placements, a clear warning about staffing changes and access to the union training fund would let me move before the savings ran out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets blamed if an AI list is wrong. A junior worker can be told the tool is accurate and then blamed for following it. I want the lead and the contractor to agree who checks a measurement before anyone makes the cut.

headlineQuote: A junior worker can be told the tool is accurate and then blamed for following it.
portrait: Amira is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker still learning after leaving school early.
Her **mortgage**, two school-age children and variable hotel income make five months saved an important but finite bridge.
She uses **AI daily** for plan questions while insisting a lead verify measurements.
She seeks **paid safety experience** and collective support before robots threaten physical site work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** quickly erases her plan-reading advantage and may cut site shifts when robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid placements**, staffing notice and a union training fund would help her move roles before savings run out.
